analysis.one_liner: Requires the EPA to designate PFAS "forever chemicals" as hazardous substances for cleanup.
analysis.headline: The bipartisan PFAS Action Act of 2019, with 52 Senate cosponsors including six Republicans, never received a committee or floor vote before the 116th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill directs the EPA to designate all PFAS chemicals — manmade "forever chemicals" used in nonstick, waterproofing, and firefighting products and found in drinking water near military bases and industrial sites — as hazardous substances under the Superfund law. That designation lets the government force parties responsible for PFAS releases to pay for cleaning up contaminated sites. The bill was introduced by Senator Tom Carper with 52 cosponsors from both parties, but it sat in committee with no action for the rest of the Congress.
analysis.who_benefits: People living with PFAS-contaminated drinking water — typically near military installations, airports, and chemical plants — gain a legal route to cleanup, because a hazardous-substance designation lets the EPA compel those responsible for the pollution to clean it up or reimburse cleanup costs. Taxpayers also benefit, since Superfund designation puts cleanup costs on polluters rather than the public.

how_it_helps.text: Requires the EPA, within one year of enactment, to designate all per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) as hazardous substances under CERCLA, the 1980 Superfund law.

A hazardous-substance designation under CERCLA is what lets the EPA order cleanup of contaminated sites and recover cleanup costs from the parties responsible for the release; without the designation, PFAS cleanup has generally been paid for voluntarily or with public money.
The bill responds to a class of chemicals that do not break down in the environment and have been found in drinking water around military bases and industrial facilities.

analysis.who_pays: Companies that manufactured PFAS or released it into the environment would bear cleanup liability under the Superfund law. Some of those costs could reach consumers through higher prices, and parties that merely handled PFAS — such as water systems — could face liability questions, since the bill covers all PFAS chemicals rather than a case-by-case list.
analysis.who_pays_short: PFAS makers and companies that released it

drawbacks.text: The bill covers "all" PFAS substances within one year — a family of thousands of related chemicals — rather than designating individual substances after case-by-case health and risk evaluation.

Under the Superfund law, cleanup liability is strict and can attach to parties who did not manufacture the chemical but whose handling of it led to a release; water and wastewater systems that received PFAS passing through their pipes could face liability and litigation costs, which could be passed to ratepayers.
Broad designation could increase costs for companies that used PFAS-containing products, such as firefighting foam at airports, with some of the cost ultimately reaching consumers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the communities whose water has been contaminated, the bill's main benefit — putting cleanup obligations and costs on the companies responsible — is substantial, and it shifts costs that otherwise fall on taxpayers. The honest cost is legal and economic uncertainty: a blanket, one-year designation of the entire PFAS family gives polluters, users, and water utilities no case-by-case process to distinguish the most dangerous chemicals from the least, and litigation over who pays for cleanup is a predictable consequence. A narrower, phased designation would have addressed that objection; the bill chose breadth and speed instead.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced with 52 bipartisan cosponsors and referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, which never acted on it, so it died without a vote when the Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Senator Tom Carper (D-DE) introduced the bill on February 28, 2019, with an initial list of 19 cosponsors including Republicans such as Shelley Moore Capito, Thom Tillis, Cory Gardner, Lisa Murkowski, and Richard Burr.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Environment and Public Works on the day it was introduced.
Over the remainder of the 116th Congress, the only action ever taken was that referral; no hearing, committee vote, or floor vote is recorded in the action history.
The bill ultimately had 52 cosponsors, including 6 Republicans, 44 Democrats, and 2 Independents.
The 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021, without the bill having come to a vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: PFAS manufacturers and the companies facing potential Superfund cleanup liability came out ahead, because a bipartisan bill that would have triggered that liability never reached a vote. Communities waiting for PFAS site cleanup and the taxpayers who fund it when polluters do not are no better off than before.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: PFAS makers and polluters facing cleanup liability

for.name: Tom Carper
for.role: U.S. Senator (D-DE), sponsor; senior member of the Environment and Public Works Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited an initial bipartisan list of 19 cosponsors from both parties.

for.name: 52 Senate cosponsors (44 Democrats, 6 Republicans, 2 Independents)
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors, giving the bill majority-of-the-Senate support, but the bill never reached a vote.

against.name: John Barrasso
against.role: Chair, Senate Environment and Public Works Committee
against.what_they_did: As committee chair, never scheduled the bill for a hearing or committee vote after its referral; the bill received no committee action for nearly two years.

against.name: Mitch McConnell
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor at any point during the 116th Congress.

against.name: American Chemistry Council
against.what_they_did: Campaigned against designating PFAS as CERCLA hazardous substances, arguing Superfund designation would impose unfair liability across the supply chain.

sides.party_line_note: Support was bipartisan: of 52 cosponsors, 6 were Republicans and 2 were Independents alongside 44 Democrats, yet the bill died without a vote in a Republican-run Senate.

industries.industry: PFAS manufacturers (e.g., makers of fluoropolymer and fluorosurfactant chemicals)
industries.note: A CERCLA hazardous-substance designation would make PFAS releases the basis for Superfund cleanup orders and cost recovery, exposing the companies that made the chemicals to cleanup liability for contaminated sites. Their interest in avoiding that liability runs directly against communities seeking cleanup.

industries.industry: Companies that used or released PFAS (firefighting foam users at airports and military sites, metal finishers, apparel and paper goods manufacturers)
industries.note: The designation extends cleanup liability to anyone responsible for a PFAS release, not just the original chemical makers, so past users of PFAS-containing products would face exposure. Their cost of cleanup is the public's gain in restored land and water.

Utilities would benefit from cleaner source water but, because the bill covers all PFAS rather than a maker-only liability scheme, systems that merely received PFAS passing through could face Superfund liability and pass the cost to ratepayers.
